description: We are Kesapattar, an international student team in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. Our project, BAIKONUR: MISSION CONTROL, is an interactive 3D simulator where players design and manage a fictional Mars orbiter mission. It combines spacecraft engineering, resource management, launch decisions, and mission operations using NASA/JPL Horizons data and NASA Mars Climate Sounder references. Our goal is to make space exploration and engineering more accessible to students.
summary: BAIKONUR: MISSION CONTROL is an interactive 3D educational simulator that puts players in charge of KAZMARS-1, a fictional Mars orbiter mission. Players define a science objective, assemble a spacecraft, compare launch and orbit options, investigate simulated pre-launch telemetry, and make mission decisions during Mars operations. The experience teaches how engineering trade-offs involving mass, power, budget, communications, and scientific goals affect mission success. It incorporates Earth–Mars and Sun–Mars geometry from NASA/JPL’s Horizons system and instrument specifications from NASA’s Mars Climate Sounder reference. By combining interactive gameplay with transparent data sources and clearly identified educational assumptions, the project makes space mission design more accessible and engaging for students. KAZMARS-1 is fictional and is not an operational spacecraft or NASA mission.
details:
Project Overview

BAIKONUR: MISSION CONTROL is an interactive 3D educational game built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, responding to the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players take the role of Mission Director of KAZMARS-1, a fictional Mars orbiter, and manage the mission from initial planning to final debrief.

How It Works

The experience is organized into seven stages:

  1. Mission Briefing: Players choose a scientific objective related to Martian climate, dust storms, or the water cycle.
  2. Spacecraft Design: Players configure a modular 3D orbiter by selecting instruments, solar arrays, antennas, data recorders, and propulsion systems.
  3. Launch Planning: Players compare fictional launch vehicles, orbital options, mission duration, and resource limits.
  4. Launch Readiness: Players investigate a simulated pressure and temperature anomaly using three evidence panels and make a Go/No-Go recommendation.
  5. Mars Operations: Players manage communications, solar power, a solar-conjunction blackout, and a simulated dust-storm response.
  6. Mission Debrief: A deterministic scoring system evaluates scientific value, resource efficiency, decision quality, and mission performance.
  7. Replay: Players can revise their decisions and explore different mission outcomes.

The simulator supports Guided and Advanced modes and pass-and-play teamwork for one to four players on a single device. It also includes a 2D fallback when WebGL is unavailable and reduced-motion settings.

NASA Data and Scientific Basis

The project uses NASA/JPL Horizons ephemeris data for Earth–Mars light time, distance, and range-rate, as well as Sun–Mars distance. These values inform communication-delay displays, simplified data-rate calculations, solar-power estimates, and the timing of the solar-conjunction scenario.

NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter Mars Climate Sounder instrument reference provides the real instrument's approximate mass (9 kg), power use (11 W), and scientific measurement context. These specifications inform the game's fictional ATMOS-S instrument.

The project distinguishes NASA-sourced information from physical constants, team-created game assumptions, and synthetic telemetry. Countdown pressure and temperature readings are generated for an educational scenario and do not represent a real launch or spacecraft.

Technology

The application was developed with React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, React Three Fiber, GSAP, Recharts, Zustand, Vitest, and Playwright. The 3D spacecraft and space environment are generated procedurally in the browser. NASA/JPL Horizons data is accessed through a server-side proxy when available, with a dated cached dataset as a fallback.

Automated checks documented in the repository include 65 passing unit tests, five passing end-to-end tests, type-checking, and a production build.

Creativity, Benefits, and Impact

The project turns abstract aerospace engineering trade-offs into interactive decisions with visible consequences. Instead of only reading about mission design, students can experiment with spacecraft configurations, compare competing constraints, investigate evidence, and learn why a mission may succeed or fail.

Its intended impact is educational: making systems engineering, planetary science, and data-informed decision-making more approachable for students. The game is not flight software, a real spacecraft design tool, or a NASA mission. Orbital, propulsion, cost, and several operational parameters are simplified educational assumptions rather than validated engineering specifications.

Team and AI-Assisted Development

The team defined the concept, educational goals, characters, scientific constraints, and acceptance criteria, and directed and reviewed the implementation. Claude Code (Anthropic) assisted with code generation, interface text, game values, tests, and documentation. No AI-generated images or videos are included; the 3D visuals are procedural and character illustrations are code-drawn vectors. Sounds are synthesized in the browser.

The project is an independent educational entry and is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.
